title: Design a globally unique ID generator.
description: Generate unique, sortable IDs across distributed systems using UUID, Snowflake, or database sequences.

data.text: **Question:** Design a service that generates globally unique IDs across distributed systems.

data.title: Functional Requirements
items: Globally unique IDs across all data centers
IDs that are safe for URLs and database keys
Support for multiple data centers and regions

data.text: Several approaches exist: UUID v4 provides randomness but is not sortable. Snowflake IDs encode timestamp, worker ID, and sequence for sortability. Database sequences guarantee uniqueness but require coordination. Multi-master allocation pre-allocates ranges to reduce coordination.

data.title: Clock Skew
data.text: Clock skew can cause duplicate or out-of-order IDs. Use NTP synchronization and reject IDs if local clock is behind the last timestamp.

data.title: Handling Clock Issues
items: Use NTP to synchronize clocks across all servers
Reject IDs if the local clock is behind the last generated timestamp
Wait for clock catchup if skew exceeds a threshold
Use a separate worker ID per server to avoid collisions
Monitor clock drift and alert on anomalies

cards.title: UUID v4
cards.description: 128-bit random identifiers. No coordination needed. Not sortable.

cards.title: Snowflake
cards.description: 64-bit sortable IDs with timestamp, worker ID, and sequence. Twitter-inspired.

cards.title: Database Sequence
cards.description: Auto-incrementing integers from a centralized database.

data.title: Horizontal Scaling Strategies
items: Use pre-allocated ID ranges to reduce coordination frequency
Assign unique worker IDs per data center and server
Replicate ID generator state for high availability
Cache recently generated IDs for low-latency access
Monitor ID consumption rates to detect allocation failures

items.question: Why not just use database auto-increment?
items.answer: Auto-increment requires a single database, creating a bottleneck and single point of failure. It does not scale across multiple data centers.

items.question: Can two Snowflake generators create the same ID?
items.answer: No, as long as each generator has a unique worker ID and the clock never goes backwards within the same millisecond.

items.question: How do you handle server restarts with Snowflake?
items.answer: Persist the last timestamp and worker ID. On restart, wait until the local clock catches up to the last timestamp before generating new IDs.

items.question: Should IDs be exposed to users?
items.answer: Avoid exposing sequential IDs in URLs. Use Snowflake or UUID to prevent enumeration attacks and information leakage about business volume.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Snowflake-style IDs provide sortable, unique identifiers without coordination
Clock synchronization is critical for timestamp-based ID generation
Pre-allocate ID ranges to reduce coordination overhead
Avoid exposing sequential IDs to prevent enumeration attacks
Use different ID strategies based on scale and coordination requirements
data.takeaway: Globally unique ID generation requires balancing uniqueness guarantees, sortability, and distributed coordination overhead.
